Mutations, Diversity, Burden and Minority Variants

A hands-on workshop using HIV-1 deep-sequencing data (NC_001802.1)

Dr. W. Choga

17 July 2026

How to use this document. Every number in the prose is computed from the data, not typed in. Run it top-to-bottom.

This is not a canned demo. Partway through, our first analysis will produce a confident, FDR-significant result that turns out to be an artefact. We will catch it, diagnose it, and fix it. That reversal is the most important thing in this workshop.

1 The dataset

A per-position pileup from a whole-genome HIV-1 deep-sequencing run, aligned to NC_001802.1 (the RefSeq HIV-1 HXB2 reference, 9,181 bp).

Column Meaning
Nucleotide pos position on the reference genome (1–9181)
Nucleotide ref the reference base at that position
Nucleotide strain the consensus base called for this sample
Depth of coverage (high quality) reads passing quality filter
A/C/G/T count (high quality) how many reads showed each base
indel count reads supporting an insertion/deletion
Depth of coverage (raw) reads before quality filtering

The A/C/G/T counts are the whole point: they let us see below the consensus, into the minority population. A consensus FASTA throws that away.

raw <- readr::read_csv(params$csv, trim_ws = TRUE, show_col_types = FALSE)

# Header has spaces/parentheses; rename positionally so the code is robust.
names(raw) <- c("pos", "ref", "strain", "depth_hq",
                "A", "C", "G", "T", "indel_count", "depth_raw")

dat <- raw %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(pos, depth_hq, A, C, G, T, indel_count, depth_raw), as.numeric),
    indel_count = replace_na(indel_count, 0),
    ref    = str_trim(ref),
    strain = str_trim(strain)
  )

dim(dat)
## [1] 9131   10
head(dat, 5)

1.1 Row types: not every row is a SNP

There are three kinds of row here, and a two-way split silently turns the third into NA:

  1. SNP-comparable — single ref base, single consensus base, real counts.
  2. indel record — multi-base ref or strain, no depth/counts.
  3. zero-coverage — empty strain: no reads at all, so no consensus could be called. These are not deletions — they were simply never sequenced.
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(row_type = case_when(
    is.na(strain) | strain == ""          ~ "zero-coverage (no call)",
    nchar(ref) == 1 & nchar(strain) == 1  ~ "SNP-comparable",
    TRUE                                  ~ "indel record"
  ))

count(dat, row_type) %>% kable(caption = "Row types in the file")
Row types in the file
row_type n
SNP-comparable 9005
indel record 26
zero-coverage (no call) 100 
snp  <- filter(dat, row_type == "SNP-comparable")
ind  <- filter(dat, row_type == "indel record")
nocv <- filter(dat, row_type == "zero-coverage (no call)")

ind %>% select(pos, ref, strain, indel_count) %>% head(8) %>%
  kable(caption = "Example indel records (multi-base ref or strain)")
Example indel records (multi-base ref or strain)
pos ref strain indel_count
279 GG G 28659
306 T TA 29226
704 ACACAGCAAT A 5961
1454 AGCT A 4303
1729 CTGGGGT T 5436
1781 ACTGTAT A 5169
5319 TT T 6476
5599 GTAC T 3829

A trap worth knowing. nchar(NA) is NA, not 0. So filter(nchar(strain) == 1) evaluates to NA for the zero-coverage rows and dplyr drops them without a word. You lose 100 rows and nothing tells you. Here they sit at positions 9082–9181 — the 3’ tail the sequencing never reached. The depth filter would have excluded them anyway, so no number below changes — but “silently dropped” and “correctly excluded” are different things, and only one of them is reproducible.

1.2 Coverage QC — before any variant calling

You cannot call a variant you did not sequence deeply enough to see.

snp %>% summarise(
  sites = n(), zero_depth = sum(depth_hq == 0),
  median_depth = median(depth_hq), min_depth = min(depth_hq), max_depth = max(depth_hq)
) %>% kable(caption = "High-quality depth summary")
High-quality depth summary
sites zero_depth median_depth min_depth max_depth
9005 0 4002 2 31797 
p_cov <- ggplot(snp, aes(pos, depth_hq)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = params$min_depth, colour = "firebrick", linetype = 2) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Coverage across the HIV-1 genome",
       subtitle = paste0("Red = analysis threshold (", params$min_depth, "x)"),
       x = "Genome position (NC_001802.1)", y = "Depth (log10)")

p_hist <- ggplot(snp, aes(depth_hq)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Depth distribution", x = "Depth (log10)", y = "Sites")

p_cov / p_hist

callable <- snp %>%
  mutate(total = A + C + G + T) %>%
  filter(depth_hq >= params$min_depth, total >= params$min_depth)

cat(sprintf("Callable sites: %s of %s (%.1f%%)\n",
            format(nrow(callable), big.mark = ","),
            format(nrow(snp), big.mark = ","),
            100 * nrow(callable) / nrow(snp)))
## Callable sites: 8,924 of 9,005 (99.1%)

Coverage is not uniform. Low-coverage sites have a worse limit of detection. “No variant found” at 500× and at 20,000× are not the same statement.

2 What is a mutation?

A mutation is a change in sequence relative to a reference. Three things must be pinned down before the word means anything:

  1. Relative to what? Reference genome? The patient’s own baseline? “Mutation” is always a comparison.
  2. In what fraction of the population? In a virus you have a population of genomes. A change in 100% of them and in 2% of them are both real — and mean different things.
  3. With what confidence? Sequencers make errors. A 0.3% signal may be a mutation or noise.

Two comparisons are available in this file:

  • ref vs strain → consensus mutations (Sanger would see these too)
  • strain vs the base counts → minority variants (deep sequencing only)

2.1 Consensus mutations (ref vs strain)

cons <- callable %>% filter(ref != strain)

cat(sprintf("Consensus mutations: %s\n", format(nrow(cons), big.mark = ",")))
## Consensus mutations: 1,287
cat(sprintf("Divergence from reference: %.2f%% of callable sites\n",
            100 * nrow(cons) / nrow(callable)))
## Divergence from reference: 14.42% of callable sites
cons %>% count(ref, strain, name = "n") %>% arrange(desc(n)) %>% head(12) %>%
  kable(caption = "Most common reference -> sample consensus changes")
Most common reference -> sample consensus changes
ref strain n
G A 269
A G 241
C T 155
T C 150
C A 99
A C 94
A T 76
T A 61
G C 39
T G 39
C G 33
G T 31

Interpretation. ~14% divergence is enormous — and expected. This sample is almost certainly a non-subtype-B virus compared against a subtype-B reference (HXB2). Most of these are subtype differences: evolution that happened long before this infection.

A difference from the reference is not a mutation that arose in your sample. The reference is a historical accident, not a wild-type ideal.

3 Types of mutation

Independent axes — do not mix them up.

3.1 By structural change

Type What happens In this file
Substitution (SNV/SNP) one base swapped ref and strain both 1 base
Insertion bases added strain longer than ref
Deletion bases removed ref longer than strain 
ind_class <- ind %>%
  mutate(
    indel_type = case_when(nchar(strain) > nchar(ref) ~ "Insertion",
                           nchar(strain) < nchar(ref) ~ "Deletion",
                           TRUE ~ "Complex/other"),
    size  = abs(nchar(ref) - nchar(strain)),
    frame = if_else(size %% 3 == 0, "In-frame (x3)", "Frameshift")
  )

count(ind_class, indel_type, frame) %>%
  kable(caption = "Indel records by type and reading-frame effect")
Indel records by type and reading-frame effect
indel_type frame n
Deletion Frameshift 4
Deletion In-frame (x3) 13
Insertion Frameshift 1
Insertion In-frame (x3) 8

Why frame matters. An indel sized in multiples of 3 adds/removes whole codons — the protein is shorter but readable. Any other size shifts the reading frame, garbling every downstream codon. Same “one mutation”, wildly different consequence.

Note most indels here are in-frame — consistent with real viral variation rather than random error, which has no reason to respect codon boundaries.

3.2 By biochemistry: transitions vs transversions

  • Transition (Ti): purine↔︎purine (A↔︎G) or pyrimidine↔︎pyrimidine (C↔︎T)
  • Transversion (Tv): purine↔︎pyrimidine

There are 8 possible transversions but only 4 transitions, so pure chance predicts Ti/Tv = 0.5. Real data runs much higher (~2 genome-wide in humans) because transitions are mechanistically favoured and more often synonymous.

Ti/Tv is your cheapest, most powerful QC metric. Remember 0.5 = the noise line. We will use this to catch an artefact in section 7.

is_transition <- function(a, b) {
  paste0(pmin(a, b), pmax(a, b)) %in% c("AG", "CT")
}

cons_titv <- cons %>%
  mutate(class = if_else(is_transition(ref, strain), "Transition", "Transversion"))

titv_tab <- count(cons_titv, class)
titv_ratio <- with(titv_tab, n[class == "Transition"] / n[class == "Transversion"])

kable(titv_tab, caption = "Consensus mutations by substitution class")
Consensus mutations by substitution class
class n
Transition 815
Transversion 472 
cat(sprintf("Consensus Ti/Tv = %.2f  (chance alone would give 0.50)\n", titv_ratio))
## Consensus Ti/Tv = 1.73  (chance alone would give 0.50)
cons %>% count(ref, strain) %>%
  mutate(class = if_else(is_transition(ref, strain), "Transition", "Transversion")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(strain, ref, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n, colour = class), size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "steelblue") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Transition" = "firebrick", "Transversion" = "grey20")) +
  labs(title = "Substitution spectrum: reference base -> sample base",
       subtitle = "Red labels = transitions (A<->G, C<->T)",
       x = "Sample (strain) base", y = "Reference base", fill = "Count", colour = NULL)

Ti/Tv ≈ 1.7 — comfortably above the 0.5 noise line. These consensus differences are real evolutionary signal.

3.3 By functional consequence (coding effect)

Requires the reading frame, so it cannot be read off a pileup alone — but it is what clinicians care about.

Class Effect on protein Example
Synonymous (silent) codon changes, amino acid does not GGA→GGG, both Gly
Missense one amino acid replaced HIV RT K103N
Nonsense codon → STOP, truncated usually lethal to the virus
Frameshift indel not ×3, downstream garbled usually knockout
Non-coding / regulatory outside genes LTR promoter

dN/dS is the classic selection test: < 1 purifying, ≈ 1 neutral, > 1 positive (diversifying) selection — the signature of immune escape and drug pressure.

3.4 By origin

Germline (inherited) vs somatic (acquired — the basis of cancer genomics). For a virus: transmitted vs acquired — which, for HIV drug resistance, decides whether a first-line regimen was ever going to work.

3.4.1 Exercise 1

Consensus Ti/Tv was ~1.7. Predict now whether the minority-variant Ti/Tv will be higher or lower, and why. Write it down before section 7.

4 How to calculate mutations

4.1 The core quantity: allele frequency (VAF)

\[\text{VAF}_{b} = \frac{n_b}{n_A+n_C+n_G+n_T}\]

Everything downstream — minority calls, diversity, burden — is built on this.

freq <- callable %>%
  mutate(across(c(A, C, G, T), ~ .x / total, .names = "f_{.col}")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    major_base = c("A", "C", "G", "T")[which.max(c(A, C, G, T))],
    major_f    = max(c(f_A, f_C, f_G, f_T)),
    minor_base = c("A", "C", "G", "T")[order(c(A, C, G, T), decreasing = TRUE)[2]],
    minor_f    = sort(c(f_A, f_C, f_G, f_T), decreasing = TRUE)[2],
    minor_n    = sort(c(A, C, G, T), decreasing = TRUE)[2]
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(change = paste0(major_base, ">", minor_base))

freq %>% select(pos, ref, strain, depth_hq, major_base, major_f, minor_base, minor_f) %>%
  head(6)

Sanity check — the file’s consensus should equal our computed majority base:

cat(sprintf("Agreement between file consensus and our majority base: %.2f%%\n",
            100 * mean(freq$major_base == freq$strain)))
## Agreement between file consensus and our majority base: 100.00%

4.2 Mutation frequency vs mutation rate — do not confuse them

Mutation frequency Mutation rate
Question How many mutants now? How fast do new ones appear?
Units proportion per base per replication
Needs one sample ≥2 timepoints, or known generations
From this file? Yes No

Frequency is a snapshot — the product of mutation and selection and drift and elapsed time. A high-frequency variant may be common because it arose often, or because it was favoured.

genome_len <- 9181
hiv_rate   <- 2.4e-5   # mutations per base per replication cycle
virions    <- 1e10     # produced per day, untreated

cat(sprintf("Expected new mutations per genome per cycle: %.2f\n", hiv_rate * genome_len))
## Expected new mutations per genome per cycle: 0.22
cat(sprintf("Every possible single-base mutation is generated ~%.0f times per day\n",
            hiv_rate * virions))
## Every possible single-base mutation is generated ~240000 times per day

That second number is the whole ballgame: every possible point mutation is created many times a day. Resistance is not a question of whether it is generated — only whether the drug gives it a reason to expand.

5 Diversity

Divergence asks “how far from the reference?”. Diversity asks “how variable is the population within itself?” A sample can be far from the reference yet uniform, or sit on the reference and be a seething swarm.

This is the quasispecies concept: an infection is not a virus, it is a cloud of related genomes.

5.1 Shannon entropy (per site)

\[H = -\sum_{b \in \{A,C,G,T\}} p_b \ln p_b\]

\(H = 0\) = invariant site. \(H = \ln 4 = 1.386\) = all four bases equally likely.

shannon <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; -sum(p * log(p)) }

div <- freq %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(H = shannon(c(f_A, f_C, f_G, f_T))) %>%
  ungroup()

cat(sprintf("Mean Shannon entropy: %.4f  (max = %.3f)\n", mean(div$H), log(4)))
## Mean Shannon entropy: 0.0262  (max = 1.386)
cat(sprintf("Sites with H > 0.1: %d\n", sum(div$H > 0.1)))
## Sites with H > 0.1: 185

5.2 Nucleotide diversity (π)

π is the probability that two randomly drawn reads differ at a site. Use the sample-size-corrected estimator:

\[\hat{\pi}_{\text{site}} = \frac{n}{n-1}\left(1 - \sum_b p_b^2\right)\]

The \(\frac{n}{n-1}\) term matters: without it, low-coverage sites look artificially less diverse purely because you sampled fewer reads.

div <- div %>%
  mutate(pi_site = (total / (total - 1)) * (1 - (f_A^2 + f_C^2 + f_G^2 + f_T^2)))

cat(sprintf("Genome-wide nucleotide diversity, pi = %.5f\n", mean(div$pi_site)))
## Genome-wide nucleotide diversity, pi = 0.00810
cat(sprintf("  i.e. two random reads differ at ~%.1f of every 10,000 bases\n",
            10000 * mean(div$pi_site)))
##   i.e. two random reads differ at ~81.0 of every 10,000 bases
ggplot(div, aes(pos, pi_site)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = pi_site > 0.02), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey70", "firebrick"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Within-host nucleotide diversity across the genome",
       subtitle = "Red = pi > 0.02",
       x = "Genome position", y = expression(pi ~ "(per site)"))

5.3 Assigning sites to genes — mind the overlapping ORFs

HIV-1 is a masterclass in genomic compression: genes overlap, in different reading frames. vpu sits inside env; rev/tat exon 2 sit inside env.

A naive case_when assigns each site to one gene and silently discards the overlaps. Use a long-format join so a site can belong to several genes.

genes <- tribble(
  ~gene,   ~start, ~end,
  "gag",     336,  1838,
  "pol",    1631,  4642,
  "vif",    4587,  5165,
  "vpr",    5105,  5396,
  "tat_e1", 5377,  5591,
  "vpu",    5608,  5856,
  "env",    5771,  8341,
  "rev_e2", 7925,  8199,
  "nef",    8343,  8963
)

# Long format: one row per (site, gene). Overlapping sites appear more than once.
long <- div %>% crossing(genes) %>% filter(pos >= start, pos <= end)

long %>% count(pos) %>% count(n, name = "n_sites") %>%
  rename(genes_per_site = n) %>%
  kable(caption = "Sites belonging to 1 vs 2 overlapping reading frames")
Sites belonging to 1 vs 2 overlapping reading frames
genes_per_site n_sites
1 7865
2 685 
gene_div <- long %>%
  group_by(gene) %>%
  summarise(sites = n(), pi = mean(pi_site), H = mean(H), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(pi))

kable(gene_div, digits = 5, caption = "Diversity by HIV-1 gene")
Diversity by HIV-1 gene
gene sites pi H
vif 579 0.01100 0.03403
vpu 240 0.01019 0.03253
rev_e2 275 0.00927 0.02880
env 2535 0.00894 0.02818
pol 3000 0.00783 0.02622
gag 1479 0.00782 0.02596
vpr 291 0.00731 0.02448
nef 621 0.00694 0.01977
tat_e1 215 0.00539 0.01886 
ggplot(gene_div, aes(reorder(gene, pi), pi)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") + coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Which HIV-1 genes carry the most within-host diversity?",
       x = NULL, y = expression("mean" ~ pi))

env sits high — the surface protein, under relentless antibody pressure, and tolerant of change. pol (drug target, structurally constrained) is lower. Diversity maps onto selection.

5.3.1 Exercise 2

Compute diversity in 100 bp windows across env only, and mark the variable loops (V1–V5). Do they stand out as peaks?

Predict first, then run it. Almost everyone predicts peaks — the loops are called variable for a reason. In this sample they do not appear: mean π in the loops is 0.00903 vs 0.00893 in the conserved regions, and by median the loops are significantly lower (Wilcoxon p = 0.004).

The loops are not conserved. The explanation is in the instrument, and env_minority_fasta.R works it through: HIV’s variable loops vary mostly in length (7 of 12 env indels sit in them — a 6.8-fold rate enrichment, Poisson p = 0.0015), and a per-position pileup is indexed by reference coordinate. It has one row per reference base and no way to say “this read carries four extra codons here.” Length variation is invisible by construction — and worse, reads carrying long indels align badly, so the loops also lose coverage (94.5% callable vs 99.4%).

The measurement, not the biology, produced the null result. Ask yourself what other questions this file cannot answer, no matter how carefully you filter it. Choosing the instrument comes before choosing the statistic.

6 Minority variants — and how to know if they are real

6.1 The idea

Sanger sequencing sees ~20% and above. Rarer variants are invisible. Deep sequencing can in principle reach 1% or below. Variants in that gap — present, real, sub-consensus — are minority variants, and in HIV they matter:

  • Minority drug-resistance mutations at 1–20% are associated with increased risk of virological failure, especially for NNRTIs (low genetic barrier).
  • They are archived or transmitted, and invisible to standard genotyping.
  • Under drug pressure a 1% variant can sweep to fixation in weeks.

6.2 First attempt: a binomial test against the error rate

If the per-base error rate is \(\varepsilon\), then under the null “this is just error” the alt count is \(\text{Binomial}(n, \varepsilon)\).

eps <- params$error_rate

minor <- div %>%
  filter(minor_n > 0) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(p_error = binom.test(minor_n, total, p = eps, alternative = "greater")$p.value) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(q_error = p.adjust(p_error, method = "BH"))

naive <- minor %>% filter(q_error < 0.01, minor_f >= params$minor_vaf)

cat(sprintf("Assumed error rate: %.1f%%\n", 100 * eps))
## Assumed error rate: 0.2%
cat(sprintf("Sites with any 2nd allele: %d\n", nrow(minor)))
## Sites with any 2nd allele: 8708
cat(sprintf("Passing VAF >= %.0f%% AND FDR < 1%%: %d\n",
            100 * params$minor_vaf, nrow(naive)))
## Passing VAF >= 1% AND FDR < 1%: 451

451 minority variants, every one of them statistically significant at FDR < 1%. A tempting result. Let us try to destroy it.

6.3 The Ti/Tv stress test — where it falls apart

Recall: Ti/Tv = 0.5 is what pure chance gives. Compute Ti/Tv as a function of the VAF threshold.

titv_at <- function(d) {
  d <- d %>% mutate(class = if_else(is_transition(major_base, minor_base), "Ti", "Tv"))
  ti <- sum(d$class == "Ti"); tv <- sum(d$class == "Tv")
  tibble(n = nrow(d), Ti = ti, Tv = tv, TiTv = ifelse(tv > 0, ti / tv, NA_real_))
}

thresholds <- c(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10)
titv_curve <- map_dfr(thresholds, ~ titv_at(filter(minor, minor_f >= .x)) %>%
                        mutate(threshold = .x)) %>%
  select(threshold, n, Ti, Tv, TiTv)

kable(titv_curve, digits = 2,
      caption = "Ti/Tv of the minor allele as a function of VAF threshold")
Ti/Tv of the minor allele as a function of VAF threshold
threshold n Ti Tv TiTv
0.00 6798 565 6233 0.09
0.00 1425 281 1144 0.25
0.01 451 151 300 0.50
0.02 129 63 66 0.95
0.03 57 29 28 1.04
0.05 20 9 11 0.82
0.10 8 4 4 1.00 
ggplot(titv_curve, aes(threshold * 100, TiTv)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = "firebrick", linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = titv_ratio, colour = "steelblue", linetype = 3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  annotate("text", x = 0.12, y = 0.58, label = "pure chance = 0.5",
           colour = "firebrick", hjust = 0, size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.12, y = titv_ratio + 0.08, label = "consensus Ti/Tv",
           colour = "steelblue", hjust = 0, size = 3.4) +
  labs(title = "Ti/Tv collapses at low VAF - the signature of error contamination",
       subtitle = "Below ~2% the 'variants' are indistinguishable from noise (or worse)",
       x = "VAF threshold (%, log scale)", y = "Ti/Tv of minor allele", size = "n sites")

This is damning. At a 0.1% threshold Ti/Tv is ~0.09 — not merely random (0.5), but far below it. Random error would give 0.5. Something worse than random is happening: a systematic, direction-specific artefact.

At our 1% threshold Ti/Tv ≈ 0.50 — exactly the chance line. Roughly half of those 451 “significant” variants are noise.

6.4 Diagnosing the artefact: look at the spectrum

bands <- minor %>%
  filter(minor_f >= 0.001) %>%
  mutate(band = cut(minor_f, c(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 1),
                    labels = c("0.1-0.5%", "0.5-1%", "1-2%", ">2%"),
                    include.lowest = TRUE))

art_sig <- c("A>C", "T>G", "G>T", "C>A")

bands %>%
  count(band, change) %>%
  group_by(band) %>% slice_max(n, n = 6, with_ties = FALSE) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(artefact = change %in% art_sig,
         lab = paste(band, change, sep = "__"),
         lab = fct_reorder(lab, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(lab, n, fill = artefact)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) sub("^.*__", "", x)) +
  facet_wrap(~ band, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "steelblue", "TRUE" = "firebrick"),
                    labels = c("plausible biology", "artefact signature"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Substitution spectrum by VAF band",
       subtitle = "Low VAF is dominated by A>C / T>G / G>T / C>A - reverse-complement pairs",
       x = NULL, y = "Sites")

Look at what dominates the low-VAF bands: A>C, T>G, G>T, C>A.

Notice these form reverse-complement pairs (A>C ≡ T>G; G>T ≡ C>A). That is the fingerprint of a chemical/technical artefact, not biology:

  • G>T / C>A is the classic 8-oxoguanine (OxoG) oxidative damage signature — introduced during library prep, e.g. by acoustic shearing.
  • A>C / T>G is a well-documented context-specific sequencing artefact.

Real biology has no reason to produce a transversion-only, strand-symmetric spectrum. Sample handling does.

6.5 Why the binomial test failed to catch it

minor %>%
  filter(minor_f >= params$minor_vaf) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_depth = median(total),
    median_alt_reads = median(minor_n),
    all_significant = mean(q_error < 0.01)
  ) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Why every 1% call passed the binomial test")
Why every 1% call passed the binomial test
n median_depth median_alt_reads all_significant
451 3465 54 1

At ~4,000× depth, a 1% variant means ~40 supporting reads. Against a null of \(\varepsilon = 0.2\%\), 40 reads is overwhelmingly significant — \(p\) is astronomically small. So the test passes every call.

The test is not wrong; its assumption is. It assumes error is uniform at 0.2% everywhere. Real error is context-specific and site-specific — at some sites it is 2%. The model cannot see that, so it confidently certifies artefacts.

The lesson: statistical significance is not biological reality. A p-value only ever tests the model you gave it. With enough depth you can get vanishingly small p-values for pure garbage. Deep sequencing does not protect you from this — it guarantees it, because depth makes everything significant.

6.6 The fix: filter the artefact signature and re-test

div <- div %>% mutate(is_artefact_sig = change %in% art_sig)

called <- div %>%
  filter(minor_n > 0, minor_f >= params$strict_vaf, !is_artefact_sig)

titv_clean <- map_dfr(c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05), function(t) {
  titv_at(div %>% filter(minor_n > 0, minor_f >= t, !is_artefact_sig)) %>%
    mutate(threshold = t)
}) %>% select(threshold, n, Ti, Tv, TiTv)

kable(titv_clean, digits = 2,
      caption = "Ti/Tv AFTER removing the artefact signature")
Ti/Tv AFTER removing the artefact signature
threshold n Ti Tv TiTv
0.01 177 151 26 5.81
0.02 75 63 12 5.25
0.05 11 9 2 4.50 
cat(sprintf("\nNaive calls (1%%, no artefact filter): %d  [Ti/Tv = %.2f]\n",
            nrow(naive), titv_at(naive)$TiTv))
## 
## Naive calls (1%, no artefact filter): 451  [Ti/Tv = 0.50]
cat(sprintf("Clean calls (%.0f%% + artefact filter):  %d  [Ti/Tv = %.2f]\n",
            100 * params$strict_vaf, nrow(called), titv_at(called)$TiTv))
## Clean calls (2% + artefact filter):  75  [Ti/Tv = 5.25]

Ti/Tv jumps from 0.50 to ~5. That is a biologically sensible number for HIV. We threw away most of our “variants” and what remains finally looks like biology.

6.7 Biological validation: the APOBEC3G signature

If the surviving calls are real, they should carry biological signal. HIV has a famous one: host APOBEC3G deaminates cytosine during reverse transcription, producing G>A hypermutation on the plus strand. vif exists precisely to destroy APOBEC3G.

If our clean variants are real, G>A should be enriched at higher VAF. Error has no reason to do that.

apobec <- minor %>%
  mutate(band = cut(minor_f, c(0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 1),
                    labels = c("<0.5%", "0.5-1%", "1-2%", "2-5%", ">5%"))) %>%
  group_by(band) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), G_to_A = sum(change == "G>A"),
            pct_GtoA = 100 * mean(change == "G>A"), .groups = "drop")

kable(apobec, digits = 1, caption = "G>A (APOBEC3G signature) by VAF band")
G>A (APOBEC3G signature) by VAF band
band n G_to_A pct_GtoA
<0.5% 7283 116 1.6
0.5-1% 976 35 3.6
1-2% 320 29 9.1
2-5% 109 22 20.2
>5% 20 4 20.0 
ggplot(apobec, aes(band, pct_GtoA)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  labs(title = "G>A rises with VAF - the APOBEC3G hypermutation signature",
       subtitle = "Sequencing error has no reason to do this. Biology does.",
       x = "Minor allele frequency band", y = "% of variants that are G>A")

G>A climbs from ~1.6% to ~20% as VAF rises. The higher-frequency variants are enriched for a specific, known, host-driven biological process. This is independent confirmation that the surviving calls are real — and that the low-VAF tier is not.

6.7.1 Exercise 3

We justified 2% empirically, from Ti/Tv and the artefact spectrum — not by convention. Now defend it to a clinician. What would you need to state alongside “we found N minority variants” for the claim to be reproducible?

7 Burden testing

7.1 What a burden test is, and why it exists

Single-variant tests work for common variants. For rare variants they fail — if a variant appears in 3 of 5,000 people, nothing has power to associate it with anything.

The burden test’s move is collapsing: stop testing variants, test units (a gene, a region, a domain).

Instead of “does variant X associate with disease?”, ask “do carriers of any rare variant in gene G differ from non-carriers?”

You trade resolution for power: you no longer know which variant matters, but you can detect that the gene matters.

Test Collapsing rule Best when
CAST binary: carries ≥1 rare variant variants rare, effects same direction
Burden / MB count, optionally weighted by rarity effects same direction
SKAT variance-component; allows mixed directions some protective, some harmful
SKAT-O data-driven blend of Burden and SKAT you don’t know which — the safe default

Critical weakness: a plain burden test assumes all variants push the same way. If half are harmful and half protective they cancel, and it sees nothing. That is why SKAT exists, and why SKAT-O is the sensible default.

7.2 An honest note on this dataset

A classical burden test compares cases vs controls across many individuals. We have one sample, so we cannot run one — be suspicious of anyone who claims otherwise.

What we can do is the same machinery in its within-sample form: collapse variants into genes and test each against a background rate. This is legitimate (it is how regional mutation-enrichment scans work in cancer genomics) and it drills the identical logic. Then we simulate a cohort for the case/control version.

7.3 Burden version 1: regional enrichment — the naive run

Null: minority variants fall uniformly at the genome-wide rate. Alternative: this gene carries more than its share.

Let us first run it on the naive 1% calls — the ones we now know are contaminated.

burden_test <- function(call_set, label) {
  bg <- nrow(call_set) / nrow(div)
  long %>%
    count(gene, name = "sites") %>%
    left_join(
      call_set %>% crossing(genes) %>% filter(pos >= start, pos <= end) %>%
        count(gene, name = "observed"),
      by = "gene"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      observed = replace_na(observed, 0),
      expected = sites * bg,
      fold     = observed / expected,
      p_value  = pbinom(observed - 1, sites, bg, lower.tail = FALSE),
      q_value  = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
      analysis = label
    ) %>%
    arrange(p_value)
}

burden_naive <- burden_test(naive, "naive (1%, no artefact filter)")

burden_naive %>%
  select(gene, sites, observed, expected, fold, p_value, q_value) %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 6, 4),
        caption = "NAIVE burden: minority variants per gene (1% threshold)")

A beautiful result! vif is enriched 1.8-fold, q < 0.001. env 1.3-fold, q < 0.001. We could write this up: “vif carries a significant excess of minority variants.”

It is wrong. vif is an artefact.

  filter(gene %in% c("vif", "env")) %>%
  select(analysis, gene, observed, fold, q_value) %>%
  arrange(gene, analysis) %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 2, 5), caption = "The verdict on vif and env")
The verdict on vif and env
analysis gene observed fold q_value
clean (2% + artefact filter) env 37 1.74 0.01090
naive (1%, no artefact filter) env 170 1.33 0.00073
clean (2% + artefact filter) vif 7 1.44 0.65348
naive (1%, no artefact filter) vif 52 1.78 0.00052

What happened.

  • vif: fold 1.8 → 1.4, q 0.0005 → non-significant. Its “enrichment” was driven by artefact-signature calls (≈77% of its 1% calls were A>C/T>G/G>T/C>A). A confident, FDR-corrected, entirely false result.
  • env: fold 1.3 → 1.7, and still significant after correction. It got stronger when noise was removed — the hallmark of real signal, and exactly what HIV biology predicts for the antibody-facing envelope protein.

The single most important slide of this workshop. Multiple-testing correction did not save us. FDR controls for chance; it is completely blind to systematic bias. Your q-value was 0.0005 and the result was still garbage. No amount of statistics rescues contaminated input.

7.5 Burden version 3: case/control (simulated cohort)

The classic design, on simulated data so the logic is visible: 20 failing, 20 suppressed; are rare variants in a gene enriched in failures?

set.seed(42)
n_case <- 20; n_ctrl <- 20; n_var <- 15

sim_gene <- function(effect) {
  rbind(
    matrix(rbinom(n_case * n_var, 1, 0.02 + effect), nrow = n_case),  # cases
    matrix(rbinom(n_ctrl * n_var, 1, 0.02),          nrow = n_ctrl)   # controls
  )
}

pheno <- c(rep(1, n_case), rep(0, n_ctrl))

run_burden <- function(G, label) {
  carrier <- as.integer(rowSums(G) > 0)          # CAST: carrier yes/no
  cast_p  <- fisher.test(table(carrier, pheno))$p.value
  load    <- rowSums(G)                          # Burden: count
  burd_p  <- summary(glm(pheno ~ load, family = binomial))$coefficients[2, 4]
  tibble(gene = label,
         mean_load_case = mean(load[pheno == 1]),
         mean_load_ctrl = mean(load[pheno == 0]),
         CAST_p = cast_p, Burden_p = burd_p)
}

bind_rows(
  run_burden(sim_gene(0.00), "null_gene (no effect)"),
  run_burden(sim_gene(0.12), "causal_gene (true effect)")
) %>%
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Simulated case/control burden: CAST vs count-based Burden")
Simulated case/control burden: CAST vs count-based Burden
gene mean_load_case mean_load_ctrl CAST_p Burden_p
null_gene (no effect) 0.2 0.3 1e+00 0.5203
causal_gene (true effect) 2.1 0.3 3e-04 0.0013

The causal gene shows a significant burden; the null gene does not. That is the engine of rare-variant association testing — the same collapsing logic we applied to genes above.

7.5.1 Exercise 4

In run_burden, make half the variants protective (flip their direction in cases). Re-run and watch the burden test’s power collapse. Then explain in one sentence why SKAT exists.

8.1 The six things to take away

  1. “Mutation” is a comparison. State: relative to what, at what frequency, with what confidence. Difference-from-reference ≠ mutation that arose in your sample — 14% of this genome differs from HXB2 because it is a different subtype, not because the patient mutated.
  2. Frequency ≠ rate. One timepoint gives a snapshot, never a speed.
  3. Diversity ≠ divergence. Independent axes — and diversity maps onto selection (env high, pol constrained).
  4. Your threshold and depth define your variant count. 451 variants at 1%, 75 at 2% with artefact filtering. Neither is “the truth” — report threshold and depth, or report nothing.
  5. Ti/Tv is your lie detector. 0.5 = noise. If your minority calls sit at 0.5, they are noise — no matter how small the p-value.
  6. Statistics cannot rescue contaminated data. We got q = 0.0005 for vif and it was pure artefact. FDR controls chance, not bias. Only the biology — Ti/Tv, the OxoG spectrum, the APOBEC signature — told us the truth.
